title: Old School
full_review:
Heavily influenced by "National Lampoon's Animal House" (1978), which put an envelope-pushing spin on college high jinks, "Old School" (DreamWorks) arrives a quarter-century later with behavior designed to titillate a more-jaded young audience.

Mitch (Luke Wilson), Frank (Will Ferrell) and Beanie (Vince Vaughn) were college pals who apparently got little out of the experience but the desire to continue partying full time forevermore.

They seem to be in their 30s. Mitch has become a real estate attorney who moves out on his current playmate (Juliette Lewis as Heidi) when he catches her engaged in kinky sex with another couple. He rents a home just off-campus from a college that seems to have very little academic activity.

The first to move in with him is Frank, a once-notorious rowdy, who has just married Marissa (Perrey Reeves), to whom he seems temperamentally unsuited. Frank's marriage lasts no longer than his first episode (in some years) of drunken public streaking, after which he takes refuge with Mitch. Beanie, a successful retail chain owner with a wife and children, sees in his pals' bachelor house an opportunity for renewed, regular debauchery.

The three old pals engage in some back-and-forth sniping with a university dean named Pritchard (Jeremy Piven), who had been their adversary and victim when he, too, was their classmate.

To avoid being evicted from the residence, which has been rezoned as campus housing, the three buddies create a would-be fraternity for sex-crazed party animals of all ages.

Their pledges include the elderly Blue (Patrick Cranshaw), whose prospective encounter with topless female wrestlers kills him.

Activity within the frat house is steeped in misogyny.

Beyond the ordinary tastelessness associated with teen sex comedies, there's an added dimension in "Old School" of college-age characters being encouraged in debauchery by characters as much as twice their age.

No one ever detours to class or cracks a book, but the film, which is full of retro jokes about homosexuals, presents an implied gay character teaching several young wives how to perform oral sex. Vulgarity reigns, from the toast at a wedding reception to the manner in which men and women relate.

Everyone seems to encourage the worst behavior in everyone else.

Those not engaged in frat-house behavior are depicted as prudes and snobs who have a tendency toward deviance in other ways.

Writer-director Todd Phillips and co-writer Scot Armstrong, who had financial success with "Road Trip" (2000), have fashioned "Old School" as a series of orgies and pranks designed to attract a predominantly young audience.

A clumsy allusion to the swimming pool scene in "The Graduate" (1967) doesn't help, although it's as clever as the new picture gets.

Performances are uniformly broad and crude. Unless it's unusually popular, "Old School" isn't the sort of credit anyone involved will be underscoring on future resumes.

Because of recurring vulgarity, graphic sexual references and content, some nudity and pervasive misogyny, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
